walkthroughs.body_html: The MPC meets eight times a year. They look at inflation (target 2%), wage growth, GDP and the labour market. If inflation is too high, they raise the rate. Cuts come during recessions. Time lag: 12–18 months for full effect.

2008 crisis showed unregulated risk-taking can crash the economy. The FCA protects consumers; the BoE's PRA ensures banks hold enough capital to absorb losses. Trade-off: tight rules may slow lending and growth.

Monetary policy: pros — fast, independent. Cons — blunt tool, hits savers/borrowers differently, time lags. Always consider: state of the economy, household debt, global context, and conflicting objectives (growth vs inflation).

mcqs.q: Are monopolies always bad for consumers?
options: Monopolies are illegal and always harmful.
A monopoly is when one country dominates world trade.
YED measures how the rich and poor differ in tastes.
Standard theory says monopolies restrict output and raise prices, but possible benefits include economies of scale, R&D investment and dynamic efficiency.

mcqs.q: What does Income Elasticity of Demand (YED) tell us?
options: The sign tells us the good type: positive YED = normal good (rises with income); negative YED = inferior good (falls with income). YED > 1 indicates a luxury; YED between 0 and 1 a necessity.
A negative YED means the demand calculation went wrong.
YED measures how the rich and poor differ in tastes.
A monopoly is when one country dominates world trade.

mcqs.q: What does the assumption 'ceteris paribus' mean in economic models?
options: YED measures how the rich and poor differ in tastes.
Ceteris paribus is a Latin name for the equilibrium price.
Ceteris paribus means everything happens at the same time in real markets.
'All other things equal' — when analysing the effect of one variable, all other variables are held constant. It is an analytical simplification, not a claim about reality.
